items.prompt: A stateful application must survive loss of one Availability Zone and keep latency low to its database. Where should the tiers be placed?
constraints: The application can run in multiple AZs.
Cross-AZ latency and cost are acceptable.

options.text: Distribute application capacity across at least two AZs and use the database's supported multi-AZ or failover topology, validating cross-AZ traffic and connection behavior.
Place all application nodes in one AZ beside the database to minimize normal latency.
Use one larger instance because an instance failure is less likely than an AZ failure.
Place replicas in the same AZ so failover never crosses an AZ boundary.

feedback.Reason: AZ distribution addresses a failure domain while the data tier supplies an appropriate failover model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An AZ is an independent failure domain within a Region; multi-AZ services and clients must be tested across that boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect deploys capacity in multiple AZs and measures normal cross-AZ path cost and failover latency.
Details.errorCorrection: Single-AZ placement trades resilience for small normal-path savings, larger instances do not remove AZ failure, and same-AZ replicas share failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multi-AZ placement can add cross-AZ transfer and coordination cost but supports availability objectives.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Single-AZ placement cannot meet an AZ-loss objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance size does not isolate the application from an AZ failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Same-AZ replicas share the failure domain.

items.prompt: A workload must keep data in a specific jurisdiction and serve local users with predictable latency. What is the first placement decision?
constraints: The service is available in multiple Regions.

options.text: Select an eligible Region that satisfies residency and service requirements, then validate user-to-Region latency, replication, DR, and data-transfer paths.
Choose the geographically closest Region without checking residency or service availability.
Store data in any Region and rely on client-side encryption to satisfy residency.
Use one Region for every user because Regions are only billing boundaries.

feedback.Reason: Region selection combines legal, service, latency, resilience, and transfer constraints.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Regions are separate geographic infrastructure domains with different service availability and network distance to users.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses an allowed Region, tests real client paths, and designs replication or backup within the residency boundary.
Details.errorCorrection: Distance alone can violate residency or feature needs, encryption does not change storage location, and Regions are more than billing labels.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A local Region can reduce user latency but may have different capacity, cost, or DR options.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Closest geography does not override legal or service constraints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Encryption does not relocate data or satisfy a location requirement by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Region choice affects latency, resilience, service availability, and data boundaries.

items.prompt: A tightly coupled HPC workload needs the lowest possible network latency among EC2 instances and can use one AZ. Which placement should be evaluated?
constraints: The application benefits from low-latency links.

options.text: Evaluate a cluster placement group, while validating capacity availability, one-AZ failure exposure, instance support, and the workload's recovery strategy.
Use a spread placement group because it always minimizes instance-to-instance latency.
Place instances randomly across Regions to maximize network locality.
Use an Auto Scaling group without placement requirements because placement is irrelevant to HPC communication.

feedback.Reason: Cluster placement groups target low-latency, high-throughput communication for suitable EC2 workloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A cluster placement group packs supported instances within a low-latency AZ network boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect weighs performance against AZ failure and capacity constraints and tests launch behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Spread placement separates instances for resilience, Regions increase latency, and generic Auto Scaling does not express placement intent.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cluster placement can improve network performance but concentrates failure and may make capacity harder to obtain.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Spread placement prioritizes failure isolation, not minimum communication latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cross-Region placement increases network distance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: HPC communication can be highly sensitive to placement and network topology.

items.prompt: A quorum service needs each instance isolated from correlated hardware failure. Which EC2 placement should be considered?
constraints: The service has at least three instances.
Failure isolation matters more than lowest network latency.
The workload can tolerate some distance.

options.text: Evaluate a spread placement group, with its instance or AZ limits and the service's quorum and recovery behavior tested.
Use a cluster placement group so all instances share the same hardware domain.
Place every instance on one host to reduce coordination latency.
Use one larger instance because multiple instances create correlated failure.

feedback.Reason: Spread placement separates instances to reduce correlated hardware or AZ failure for small critical groups.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Spread placement attempts to place instances on distinct underlying hardware and can be AZ scoped or partition scoped.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner verifies placement limits and combines it with quorum, AZ, and replacement testing.
Details.errorCorrection: Cluster placement intentionally concentrates instances, one host increases correlation, and one larger instance is not quorum isolation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Spread placement improves isolation but has instance limits and may constrain launch capacity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cluster placement trades isolation for low-latency packing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One host creates maximum correlated failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A larger instance does not provide independent quorum members.

items.prompt: A distributed service needs multiple groups of instances isolated from one another while preserving some group-local communication. Which placement should be evaluated?
constraints: The application can understand group membership.

options.text: Evaluate a partition placement group and map partitions to the service's quorum or sharding model, while testing AZ and underlying-hardware failure assumptions.
Use one cluster placement group for all partitions because isolation reduces performance.
Use one spread group for unlimited instances without checking its limits.
Place all groups in one AZ because partitions are logical only.

feedback.Reason: Partition placement groups expose separate partitions for workloads that need structured failure isolation and scale.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Instances in different partitions are isolated from failures that could affect one partition, while a partition can contain multiple instances.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect aligns application shards with placement partitions and validates the actual failure boundary.
Details.errorCorrection: Cluster packing defeats partition isolation, spread has different limits, and an AZ is still a shared domain.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Partition placement provides scalable isolation but requires application awareness and launch planning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cluster placement intentionally packs instances rather than separating partitions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Spread placement has documented limits and is not unlimited.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Logical partitions still depend on physical and AZ failure domains.

items.prompt: A high-volume application reads a database in another AZ for every request. What should be reviewed?

options.text: Measure cross-AZ latency and transfer, compare local read replicas or cache placement with the consistency requirement, and preserve AZ failure resilience.
Move every resource into one AZ to eliminate all transfer cost regardless of availability objectives.
Ignore the path because AZs are physically identical to one subnet.
Use a public IP for the database so the path becomes faster.

feedback.Reason: Cross-AZ access can affect latency and cost, but eliminating it by co-locating everything may violate resilience.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AZs are separate failure domains and cross-AZ data transfer and network hops can be material for high-volume paths.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect keeps redundant capacity and optimizes hot reads with local replicas, caching, or request routing.
Details.errorCorrection: Single-AZ co-location creates a shared failure domain, AZs are not one subnet, and public addressing is not a performance fix.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Locality can reduce normal-path cost and latency while redundant cross-AZ capacity preserves availability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Eliminating cross-AZ traffic can sacrifice required availability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: AZ separation affects both failure and network paths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public database exposure does not make the path safer or necessarily faster.

items.prompt: Users in a metropolitan area need very low latency to an application, but the primary Region is far away. Which placement should be considered?
constraints: The workload is supported in the target location.
The application can use a regional control plane.

options.text: Evaluate an AWS Local Zone for latency-sensitive resources, validating service support, data transfer, regional dependencies, capacity, and recovery back to the parent Region.
Use a second Region without comparing the user-to-Region path or data residency.
Place the application in an Availability Zone because AZs are always located in every city.
Use a larger instance in the distant Region because instance size changes geographic latency.

feedback.Reason: Local Zones extend selected AWS infrastructure closer to users for supported latency-sensitive workloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A Local Zone is an AWS infrastructure deployment associated with a parent Region, with a selected service set and its own network and capacity considerations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests the end-to-end user path and designs regional control, backup, and failure behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: A second Region may be farther or violate requirements, AZs are not city-wide, and instance size does not change distance.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Local Zones can reduce user latency but add placement, service-support, transfer, and operational complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Region choice must be based on measured path and constraints, not just count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Availability Zones are not deployed in every city.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Compute size does not reduce geographic network distance.

items.prompt: A factory needs compute and storage on site because control traffic cannot tolerate a WAN round trip. Which option should be evaluated?
constraints: The site has power and networking.
The workload has local data needs.

options.text: Evaluate AWS Outposts for supported AWS resources on premises, validating local network, capacity, service support, operations, and the dependency on the parent Region.
Use a distant Region and increase the instance size to remove WAN latency.
Use CloudFront for stateful factory control loops.
Use a public subnet in the Region and assume public routing is local to the factory.

feedback.Reason: Outposts brings supported AWS infrastructure closer to on-premises workloads where local processing and data requirements matter.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Outposts runs selected AWS services at a customer site while remaining integrated with a parent Region and local network.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates rack capacity, site operations, service APIs, control-plane connectivity, and local failure behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Instance size does not remove WAN distance, CloudFront is not a stateful compute placement, and a Region public subnet is not physically local.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: On-premises placement reduces local latency but adds hardware, capacity, connectivity, and lifecycle responsibility.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Compute size does not remove a geographic network round trip.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CDN caching is not a local stateful control loop runtime.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public routing from a Region remains geographically remote.

items.prompt: A 5G application needs ultra-low-latency processing near mobile users and uses a supported carrier location. What should be assessed?

options.text: Evaluate AWS Wavelength Zones for supported edge resources, measuring device-to-application latency, carrier connectivity, regional dependencies, and data movement.
Use an S3 bucket in the Region because object storage is always at the mobile edge.
Use a Local Zone without checking the carrier or service model.
Place the workload in any Region and tune TCP buffers to eliminate geographic latency.

feedback.Reason: Wavelength Zones place supported resources in carrier locations for mobile edge latency.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Wavelength integrates selected AWS resources with 5G carrier networks while relying on a parent Region for broader services and control.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner validates carrier route, edge capacity, regional fallback, and application partitioning.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 is not automatically at the mobile edge, Local Zone has a different placement model, and transport tuning cannot remove distance.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Wavelength can reduce device latency but narrows service choices and adds carrier and regional dependencies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Object storage Region placement does not imply mobile-edge execution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Local Zone and Wavelength have different locations and network models.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Protocol tuning cannot remove geographic propagation delay.

items.prompt: Average request latency is acceptable but users report periodic pauses. Which measurement should drive placement decisions?
constraints: Tail latency matters to the product.

options.text: Measure end-to-end and hop-level p50, p95, and p99 latency with request volume and failure correlation before changing Region, AZ, or edge placement.
Use only the arithmetic average because tails are network noise.
Move all resources to the nearest location without collecting a baseline.
Increase instance size because tail latency always indicates insufficient CPU.

feedback.Reason: Tail latency can be hidden by averages and may come from a specific hop, queue, or dependency.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Percentiles expose distribution tails; correlation with traces and network metrics identifies where pauses occur.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect compares placement alternatives using representative traffic and preserves a measurable SLO.
Details.errorCorrection: Averages hide outliers, moving without evidence can worsen other paths, and CPU is only one possible source.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Detailed measurement requires instrumentation but prevents costly geographic changes based on anecdotes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Tail latency is often the user-visible failure and is not noise by default.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Nearest is not always fastest or compliant and needs a baseline.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network queues, dependencies, and placement can dominate CPU.

items.prompt: A private workload calls a regional service endpoint from multiple AZs. What placement question matters for performance and cost?

options.text: Check whether the endpoint or service has zonal locality, measure cross-AZ data and latency, and place or route clients to the supported low-cost path without sacrificing availability.
Assume every regional endpoint is physically local to each AZ.
Route service traffic through a public internet gateway to avoid all internal hops.
Move the application into one AZ regardless of its availability requirement.

feedback.Reason: Regional service names do not guarantee identical zonal paths or transfer economics.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Private endpoints and AWS service paths can have AZ-specific placement or cross-AZ behavior that should be verified for the service.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures endpoint path and chooses endpoint placement or route tables intentionally.
Details.errorCorrection: Regional does not mean every packet stays in the source AZ, internet paths do not remove internal design, and single-AZ co-location can violate resilience.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Zonal locality can reduce transfer cost but may require multiple endpoints and health handling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Endpoint path and service behavior need service-specific verification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public routing increases exposure and is not a generic performance optimization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Single-AZ placement trades away failure-domain resilience.

items.prompt: Global users need local writes and the application can resolve conflicts. What placement model should be evaluated?
constraints: Data ownership or conflict rules exist.

options.text: Evaluate active-active regional cells with latency-aware routing, local data access, replication lag, conflict policy, and regional failover testing.
Send every user to the nearest Region without defining data conflict behavior.
Assume a global endpoint makes cross-Region writes synchronous.
Keep a single writer in one Region and label the design active-active.

feedback.Reason: Active-active placement can reduce user latency but requires explicit replication and conflict semantics.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Regional cells serve local traffic and exchange data asynchronously or through service-specific global replication mechanisms.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect assigns ownership, chooses routing and failover, and measures replicated correctness and lag.
Details.errorCorrection: Nearest routing alone can create conflicts, a global endpoint does not imply synchronous writes, and one writer is active-passive.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Active-active improves locality and regional availability but adds significant data and operational complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Routing does not resolve concurrent data writes by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A global entry point does not make application data writes synchronous.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One writer does not provide active-active writes.

items.prompt: A large multi-tenant system must prevent one regional or workload failure from spreading to all users. Which topology should be compared?
constraints: Tenants can be assigned to cells.

options.text: Evaluate cell-based regional or AZ placement with isolated capacity, data and queues, routing ownership, and controlled cell failure testing.
Use one shared database and queue because consolidation always limits blast radius.
Place all tenants in one Region and rely on security groups for workload isolation.
Use random routing so failures cannot be associated with a cell.

feedback.Reason: Cells reduce blast radius by isolating capacity and dependencies behind explicit routing boundaries.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A cell is a repeatable unit of resources and data that can fail or be operated independently from other cells.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner assigns tenants, monitors cell health, and tests routing away from one failed cell.
Details.errorCorrection: Shared stores concentrate blast radius, security groups do not isolate service failure, and random routing prevents controlled containment.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cells improve resilience and scaling boundaries but require routing, duplication, and operational automation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Shared dependencies can spread failure across all tenants.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One Region and security groups do not create independent failure cells.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Random routing is not an isolation or recovery policy.

items.prompt: A latency-based DNS policy sends many users to a Region that is healthy but overloaded. What additional signal is needed?

options.text: Combine endpoint health with regional capacity or application latency signals and bounded routing weights, then test DNS TTL and failover behavior.
Use geographic distance alone because the nearest Region is always fastest under load.
Set all Regions to equal weight regardless of capacity or health.
Reduce DNS TTL to zero and assume clients immediately use the best Region.

feedback.Reason: Latency-aware routing needs both path and capacity information; DNS caching also limits reaction speed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Route 53 policies use configured health and routing inputs, while resolvers and clients cache answers for TTL durations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator weights regions based on safe capacity and verifies how quickly clients follow a change.
Details.errorCorrection: Nearest can be overloaded, equal weights ignore capacity, and zero TTL does not guarantee immediate cache expiration everywhere.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower TTL improves agility but increases DNS query volume and still cannot control already-cached clients.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Geographic proximity does not guarantee current capacity or path quality.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Equal weighting can overload a smaller or degraded Region.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS TTL is a cache hint, not a universal immediate invalidation mechanism.

items.prompt: An internal service is consumed by workloads in three AZs and must avoid a single-AZ endpoint dependency. What topology should be checked?
constraints: The service supports multiple endpoint interfaces.

options.text: Evaluate endpoint placement in the required AZs, private DNS behavior, security-group access, health, and cross-AZ cost before choosing a single or multi-endpoint design.
Create one endpoint in one AZ because regional DNS always keeps traffic local.
Expose the service publicly so clients can choose an internet edge.
Place endpoints in every subnet without checking quotas or route associations.

feedback.Reason: Private endpoint placement can affect AZ dependency, path, cost, and availability and must be verified for the service.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Interface endpoints create ENIs in selected subnets and use private DNS and security groups for access.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses endpoint count from traffic and failure requirements and validates DNS resolution from each AZ.
Details.errorCorrection: One endpoint can create a zonal dependency, public exposure is unnecessary, and indiscriminate endpoint creation can hit quotas and cost limits.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multiple endpoints improve locality and AZ independence but add hourly and management cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Regional naming does not guarantee local endpoint placement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public access increases exposure and is not required for private service consumption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Endpoints need quota, subnet, route, DNS, and cost planning.

items.prompt: A workload relies on a private IP attached to an ENI and the instance is replaced. What should be verified?
constraints: The ENI can be detached and attached.
The subnet is in one AZ.
Security groups and routes reference the ENI.

options.text: Verify the replacement is in the ENI's AZ and that attachment, private address, security groups, routes, DNS, and health checks behave as intended.
Attach the ENI to an instance in another AZ because ENIs are regional resources.
Assume the private IP follows the instance automatically without ENI ownership.
Use the ENI as a route table because network interfaces forward all VPC traffic by default.

feedback.Reason: ENIs and their primary private addresses are AZ-scoped resources whose lifecycle affects replacement and service identity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An ENI is associated with a subnet and AZ and can carry private addresses and security groups when attached to supported resources.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner automates same-AZ replacement and validates attachment timing and dependency resolution.
Details.errorCorrection: An ENI cannot be freely attached across AZs, an instance address is not automatically a service identity, and ENIs are not route tables.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: ENI-based identity can simplify failover within an AZ but does not replace multi-AZ architecture.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: ENIs are associated with an AZ through their subnet.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Address lifecycle depends on the ENI and attachment model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An ENI is an interface, not a generic route-table target.

items.prompt: An application is deployed in a Local Zone but its control and data services remain in the parent Region. What must the design document?
constraints: The Local Zone can lose connectivity.

options.text: Document which operations depend on the parent Region, local data and control behavior during disconnection, recovery or fallback, and the measured RTO and RPO.
Assume the Local Zone is fully independent of the parent Region after deployment.
Move the control plane to a public IP so it is always reachable.
Ignore dependency failure because placement close to users guarantees availability.

feedback.Reason: Edge placement reduces latency but does not remove dependencies on regional control, data, or recovery services.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Local Zones are associated with a parent Region and supported services can have regional control and connectivity dependencies.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests disconnection, preserves local safe operation where possible, and defines recovery or traffic fallback.
Details.errorCorrection: Edge locations are not automatically independent, public addresses do not create control-plane availability, and geographic proximity is not an availability guarantee.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Edge placement can improve latency while increasing dependency and recovery design work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Local Zones remain integrated with their parent Region and service dependencies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public access does not solve control-plane dependency or security.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Placement and availability are separate design dimensions.

items.prompt: A secondary Region is used for disaster recovery and asynchronously replicates data. Which latency matters to the RPO?

options.text: Measure replication lag distribution, source and destination throughput, network interruptions, promotion time, and application reconciliation rather than assuming geographic distance alone defines RPO.
Use the shortest geographic distance as a guaranteed maximum lag.
Assume a healthy destination Region means all writes are already replicated.
Increase destination storage and assume it removes network replication delay.

feedback.Reason: RPO is determined by observed and tested replication behavior, not only map distance or destination health.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Asynchronous replication depends on data generation, service throughput, network path, backpressure, and destination apply rate.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner alarms on lag and rehearses failover with a measured loss and reconciliation procedure.
Details.errorCorrection: Distance is not a bound, destination health does not prove freshness, and storage does not remove network or apply latency.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A farther Region may provide better failure independence while increasing replication latency and cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Geographic distance is only one component and not a guaranteed lag bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Regional availability does not imply current replicated data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Storage capacity does not remove the replication path delay.

items.prompt: A service spans three AZs but one AZ has no spare capacity during an expansion. What should be included in placement planning?

options.text: Maintain per-AZ capacity headroom or a tested rebalance strategy, and validate quotas, instance availability, launch constraints, and reduced-AZ operation.
Assume Auto Scaling can always launch the same instance type in every AZ.
Concentrate all new capacity in the full AZ because it is already healthy.
Disable AZ balancing so the service can silently become single-homed.

feedback.Reason: Multi-AZ placement requires capacity and quota planning in each failure domain, not only a nominal subnet count.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Instance type capacity, quotas, and subnet addresses can differ by AZ; Auto Scaling placement is constrained by available capacity and policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner reserves headroom, tests replacement with one AZ unavailable, and chooses explicit rebalance or degradation behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Auto Scaling cannot guarantee capacity, adding to a full AZ worsens concentration, and disabling balancing hides a resilience loss.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Headroom costs more but prevents an expansion or recovery from collapsing into one AZ.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Capacity and quotas vary by AZ and instance type.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Concentrating capacity increases failure-domain exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Silent single-homing violates the multi-AZ objective.

items.prompt: A static asset is slow for global users, while application state remains in one Region. Which placement should be evaluated first?

options.text: Evaluate CloudFront caching for static or cacheable responses and keep dynamic state on the authoritative regional service with explicit cache and invalidation rules.
Move the transactional database to every edge location for every asset request.
Use an EC2 placement group across continents for global asset delivery.
Disable caching because edge locations cannot serve consistent static objects.

feedback.Reason: CDN edge caching addresses cacheable content without replicating transactional state to every edge.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFront serves cached objects from edge locations and forwards misses to an origin according to cache and invalidation policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect classifies content, sets TTLs and invalidations, and retains dynamic authorization at the origin where needed.
Details.errorCorrection: Replicating a database to every edge is excessive, placement groups are regional EC2 constructs, and edge caching can be consistent within its configured policy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Caching lowers user latency and origin load but introduces freshness and invalidation behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Transactional state does not need to be replicated to every edge to accelerate static assets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EC2 placement groups do not provide global content delivery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CDN consistency is controlled through TTL and invalidation, not impossible by definition.

items.prompt: A design reduces cross-AZ transfer by co-locating tiers, but the database and application now share one failure domain. What is the correct decision?
constraints: The organization can pay for redundancy.

options.text: Choose placement from the measured availability and latency SLOs, retaining multi-AZ redundancy and optimizing hot paths with local reads or caching where justified.
Choose one AZ because transfer cost is always more important than availability.
Use public routing to avoid the cost of redundant AZs.
Remove health checks because co-location makes failures impossible.

feedback.Reason: Cost locality is a tradeoff, not a reason to erase a required failure boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Multi-AZ redundancy and cross-AZ transfer have opposing cost and resilience effects; caching or local reads can reduce volume without removing redundancy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner preserves the SLO and measures where locality optimization gives value.
Details.errorCorrection: One AZ makes failure correlated, public routing is not a redundancy strategy, and health checks remain necessary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Redundancy costs more but may be required for the product's RTO and availability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Availability requirements must be honored alongside transfer cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public routing does not create redundant private capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Co-location increases shared failure risk rather than eliminating it.

items.prompt: A placement proposal lists Regions and AZs but does not explain user latency, dependency paths, failure domains, capacity, or data movement. What should the review require?
constraints: The service has latency and availability objectives.
Data movement has cost and compliance implications.
Edge or hybrid options are possible.

options.text: Map user and service paths, fault boundaries, capacity and quota headroom, data residency and transfer, dependency locality, observability, and tested failover behavior before approving placement.
Approve the closest Region because geographic distance fully determines performance and resilience.
Place all resources together to minimize every network hop regardless of failure objectives.
Add edge locations without defining which data or compute can run there.

feedback.Reason: Placement is an end-to-end topology decision spanning latency, failure, capacity, data, and operations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Region, AZ, Local Zone, Outposts, and Wavelength choices create different network and control-plane boundaries.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect compares alternatives against measured SLOs and tests the path under dependency and location failure.
Details.errorCorrection: Distance alone misses capacity and compliance, co-location can destroy resilience, and edge locations are not generic compute without a service model.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More deliberate placement work prevents hidden latency and shared-failure assumptions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Distance is only one factor in latency, capacity, and resilience.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Co-location reduces some hops but increases correlated failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Edge choices require explicit workload, data, and service support boundaries.
